Imperial willows wreathed in mist brushed the banners, and palace flowers heavy with dew greeted swords and halberds. Amid the fragrance of heaven, jade hairpins and vermilion slippers thronged the crimson courtyard; To the strains of celestial music, embroidered jackets and brocade robes attended the imperial carriage. Pearled curtains were rolled up, revealing the golden palanquin within the golden hall; Fans of phoenix feathers spread open, and the jeweled carriage halted before the white jade steps. Faintly the ceremonial whip cracked three times, and rank upon rank the civil and military officials stood ordered in their two columns.

p.src: Then an officer of the hall called out, “Those with matters to report, step forth and speak at once; those with none, roll up the curtain and dismiss the court.” From among the serried ranks, Chancellor Zhao Zhe and Vice Councillor Wen Yanbo stepped forward and memorialized: “At present a virulent plague is sweeping the capital, taking a grievous toll among soldiers and commoners. We humbly beseech Your Majesty to remit offenses and extend mercy, reduce punishments and lighten taxes, so as to avert Heaven’s calamity and bring relief to the myriad people.” On hearing their memorial, the emperor urgently commanded the Hanlin Academy to draft an edict forthwith: on the one hand, an amnesty was proclaimed for prisoners throughout the realm, and all taxes and levies owed by the people were remitted; on the other, the Daoist temples and Buddhist monasteries of the capital were ordered to conduct meritorious rites to avert the disaster. Unexpectedly, however, the plague grew still fiercer that year. When Emperor Renzong learned of this, he became deeply troubled and once more convened the officials to deliberate. From the ranks of officials, a great minister crossed out of his place and addressed the throne. The emperor looked and saw that it was Fan Zhongyan, Vice Director of State Affairs. After completing his obeisance and formal greeting, Fan memorialized: “At present Heaven-sent calamity rages, and soldiers and commoners alike are plunged into misery, unable to sustain their lives from one day to the next. In my humble opinion, to avert this disaster Your Majesty should summon the Celestial Master, successor to the Han lineage, to attend court without delay. Within the forbidden precincts of the capital he should conduct a Great Offering to All Heaven in three thousand six hundred divisions and report our plea to the Supreme Emperor; thus may the pestilence among the people be averted.” Emperor Renzong approved the memorial. He urgently ordered a Hanlin Academician to compose an edict, which the emperor inscribed in his own hand, and also bestowed a stick of imperial incense. He appointed Hong Xin—Intendant of Affairs within and without the palace and Grand Commandant of the Palace Front—as imperial envoy, commanding him to proceed to Dragon-Tiger Mountain in Xinzhou, Jiangxi, and summon the Reverend Zhang, Celestial Master and successor to the Han lineage, to attend court with all speed and pray for the plague to be averted. There in the Golden Hall he lit the imperial incense and personally entrusted the vermilion edict to Grand Commandant Hong, who immediately set out upon his journey.

p.src: Now Grand Commandant Hong Xin, bearing the imperial edict, traveled onward with his company. After many days upon the road, they reached Xinzhou in Jiangxi. Officials high and low came beyond the city walls to welcome him; they then dispatched a messenger to inform the abbot and Daoist community of the Shangqing Palace on Dragon-Tiger Mountain, so that they might prepare to receive the edict. The following day, all the officials escorted the grand commandant to the foot of Dragon-Tiger Mountain. There they found the many Daoists of the Shangqing Palace descending to welcome the vermilion edict, ringing bells and beating drums, bearing incense, flowers, lamps, candles, banners, pennants, and jeweled canopies, while celestial music sounded all around. The procession continued to the front of the Shangqing Palace, where the grand commandant dismounted. When the grand commandant beheld the halls and buildings, he saw that this was indeed a magnificent Shangqing Palace! There one could see:

p.src: Green pines twisted and curved, while emerald cypresses cast a deep shade. Above the gate hung an imperial plaque inscribed in gold, and by the doors were ranged sacred talismans traced in jade seal-script. Beside the Altar of the Vacant Sovereign, drooping willows and celebrated flowers showed faintly through the haze; Around the alchemical furnace, ancient pines and old junipers appeared and vanished amid the greenery. In the left wing, heavenly warriors and mighty guardians attended the Perfect Lord Taiyi; On the right, jade maidens and golden youths clustered around the Great Emperor Ziwei. Hair unbound and sword in hand, the Perfect Warrior of the North trod upon tortoise and serpent; Slippers on his feet and cap upon his head, the Old Man of the Southern Pole subdued dragon and tiger. In front stood the stellar lords of the Twenty-Eight Lodges; behind were arrayed the thirty-two celestial emperors. Below the stone steps, running water murmured; beyond the courtyard walls, fair mountains encircled the palace. Cranes bore cinnabar crowns, and tortoises grew green hair. Gray apes in the treetops offered fruit, and white deer among the sedges carried sacred fungus in their mouths. In the Hall of the Three Pure Ones, Daoists struck golden bells and paced the void; Before the Hall of the Four Saints, perfected adepts sounded jade chimes and worshiped the Dipper. Upon the steps of the incense-offering terrace, rosy clouds cast their light across azure glazed tiles; Over the jasper altar for summoning divine generals, the red sun’s reflection shimmered on crimson agate. Auspicious clouds had appeared outside the gate at dawn; one might have thought the Celestial Master was escorting Lord Lao himself.

p.src: At once, from the reverend abbot down to the Daoist acolytes and attendants, all welcomed the party in front and guided it from behind, conducting them into the Hall of the Three Pure Ones. There they received the edict and enshrined it in the place of honor at the center. Grand Commandant Hong asked the reverend overseer of the palace, “Where is the Celestial Master now?” The reverend abbot stepped forward and replied, “Your Excellency should know that the patriarch of this generation is styled the Celestial Master Xujing. By nature he loves purity and lofty solitude and has grown weary of welcomes and farewells. He built himself a thatched hermitage atop Dragon-Tiger Mountain, where he cultivates the Way and nurtures his nature; therefore he does not reside in this palace.” The grand commandant said, “The emperor has now issued a summons. How am I to obtain an audience with him?” The reverend replied, “Permit me to explain. For the time being, the imperial edict must remain enshrined here in the hall; even we poor followers of the Way would not dare open and read it. Please first come to the abbot’s quarters and take tea, and then we may trouble ourselves to discuss the matter further.” The vermilion edict was accordingly enshrined in the Hall of the Three Pure Ones, and the grand commandant went with all the officials to the abbot’s quarters. The grand commandant took the central seat. The attendants served tea and then presented a vegetarian feast furnished with delicacies from both land and water. When the meal was over, the grand commandant again asked the reverend, “Since the Celestial Master is in a hermitage atop the mountain, why not send someone to invite him down to meet me, so that the vermilion edict may be formally proclaimed?” The reverend replied, “Although the patriarch of this generation dwells atop the mountain, his attainment in the Way is extraordinary. He can ride the mists and summon the clouds, and his whereabouts are never fixed. Even we seldom have the good fortune to see him. How could we order anyone to bring him down?” The grand commandant said, “If that is so, how am I ever to see him? A virulent plague now rages in the capital. His Present Majesty specially dispatched this humble official bearing an imperial edict written by the sovereign’s own hand and personally entrusted me with dragon incense, that I might invite the Celestial Master to perform a Great Offering to All Heaven in three thousand six hundred divisions, avert Heaven’s calamity, and save the myriad people. What is to be done if matters stand thus?” The reverend replied, “If the emperor wishes to save the myriad people, there is only one way. Your Excellency must summon up a truly sincere heart, fast and bathe, exchange your robes for plain cloth, and take no attendant. Carrying the edict yourself and burning the imperial incense, you must climb the mountain on foot, offer reverence, and humbly entreat the Celestial Master. Only then may you be granted an audience. If your heart lacks true sincerity, you will make the journey in vain and still find it difficult to see him.” When the grand commandant heard this, he said, “I have eaten no meat since leaving the capital; how could my heart be anything but sincere? Since that is what must be done, I shall follow your counsel and ascend the mountain at first light tomorrow.” That evening, each retired to rest for the time being. At the fifth watch the next morning, the Daoists arose and prepared fragrant hot water. They invited the grand commandant to rise and bathe, then dressed him in a fresh suit of plain cloth and put hemp shoes and straw sandals upon his feet. After he had eaten a vegetarian meal, they brought forth the vermilion edict, wrapped it in a yellow silk bundle, and placed it upon his back. In his hand he carried a silver incense burner, in which the imperial incense smoldered steadily. The assembled Daoists escorted him to the rear of the mountain and pointed out the path. The reverend again said, “Your Excellency seeks to save the myriad people. Harbor no thought of turning back; simply press upward with a sincere heart.”

p.src: Its roots are anchored in the corners of the earth, its summit touching the heart of heaven. Seen from afar, it cleaves the ragged traces of cloud; viewed close at hand, it calmly swallows the bright moon’s soul. Uneven heights are called mountains; sideward rocks pierced by passages are called mountain caves. A lone, rugged ridge is called a path; a broad, level height above is called a summit. A rounded crown with a mighty base is called a peak; a place concealing tigers and leopards is called a lair. A place hiding wind and cloud is called a crag; a retreat where lofty men dwell is called a grotto. A domain with bounds and borders is called a prefecture; a track where woodcutters come and go is called a trail. A way broad enough for carts and horses is called a road; sounding running water is called a ravine stream. The source of an ancient ford is called a brook; water dripping from rocky cliffs is called a spring. The cliff on the left screens it; the cliff on the right sets it off. What issues forth is cloud; what it gathers in is mist. Needle-pointed, it seems small; jagged and steep, it appears sheer; overhanging the void, it looks perilous; clean-hewn, it seems level. A thousand peaks vie in beauty, ten thousand ravines race with flowing water; waterfalls fly aslant, and wisteria and creepers hang inverted. When tigers roar, wind rises at the valley mouth; when apes cry, the moon sinks toward the mountainside. It is as though dark-blue pigment had dyed a thousand blocks of jade, and emerald gauze veiled ten thousand banks of smoke.

p.src: Grand Marshal Hong went on alone for a while, winding around slopes and turning along paths, clutching creepers and climbing vines. After crossing several ridges and covering more than two or three li, his feet were growing sore, his legs weak, and he could scarcely walk farther. Though he said nothing aloud, he wavered inwardly and thought, “I am a high official of the imperial court. In the capital I sleep upon layered cushions and dine from rows of cauldrons, yet even then I still feel weary. When have I ever worn straw sandals and traveled mountain roads like these! Who knows where that Celestial Master may be, while he makes this official endure such hardship!” Before he had gone another thirty or fifty paces, his shoulders heaved and he was gasping for breath. Suddenly a gust rose in a hollow of the mountain. As it passed, behind a pine tree came a roar like rushing thunder, and with a bound there sprang out a great striped tiger, white-browed and goggle-eyed. Grand Marshal Hong started in terror and cried, “Ah!” With a thud, he toppled backward. Stealing a glance at the tiger, he saw:

p.src: Its coat was one sweep of golden hue; its claws displayed eighteen hooks of silver. Its eyes were lightning, its tail a whip; its mouth a basin of blood, its teeth halberds. It stretched its loins and spread its limbs in ferocious might; it lashed its tail and shook its head with a thunderous roar. Every fox and hare upon the mountain hid away; all the roebucks and does below the ravine vanished from sight.

p.src: The tiger faced Grand Marshal Hong, circling left and wheeling right as it roared for a time; then suddenly it leapt away down the rear slope of the mountain. Grand Marshal Hong lay beneath the roots of a tree, so frightened that all thirty-six of his teeth paired off and fought each other. His heart clattered like fifteen buckets jerking up and down in a well; his whole body was numb as if stricken with palsy, his legs resembled those of a cock defeated in battle, and he cried out over and over in misery.

p.src: The great serpent darted straight to the broad rock and coiled itself in a heap before Grand Marshal Hong. Golden light burst from its two eyes; it opened its enormous mouth, thrust out its tongue, and sprayed poisonous breath into his face, terrifying the Grand Marshal until his three ethereal souls scattered and his seven bodily spirits drifted away. After watching Grand Marshal Hong for a while, the serpent streaked down the mountain and was gone in an instant. Only then did the Grand Marshal manage to scramble up, saying, “What a mercy! It frightened this official to death!” Looking over his body, he found gooseflesh larger than dumplings. He cursed the Daoist, saying, “That insufferably discourteous fellow has made sport of this official and subjected me to such terrors! If I fail to find the Celestial Master upon the mountain, I shall have words with him when I go back down.” He picked up the silver handled censer once more and straightened the imperial edict upon his person, together with his robes and headcloth, preparing to climb the mountain again. Just as he was about to step forward, he heard the faint sound of a flute behind the pine trees, drawing gradually nearer. When the Grand Marshal looked closely, he saw a young Daoist attendant riding backward upon a yellow ox, playing an iron flute held crosswise as he rounded the mountain hollow. p.src: The young Daoist attendant came over the mountain, smiling as he rode the yellow ox and played his iron flute crosswise. On seeing him, Grand Marshal Hong called out, “Where have you come from? Do you know who I am?” The young attendant paid him no heed and simply went on playing the flute. The Grand Marshal questioned him several times. The young attendant laughed aloud, took the iron flute from his lips, pointed it at Grand Marshal Hong, and said, “Have you come here, perhaps, to see the Celestial Master?” The Grand Marshal was astonished and said, “You are only a cowherd boy. How could you know that?” The young attendant laughed and said, “This morning I was attending the Celestial Master in his thatched hermitage, and I heard him say, ‘His present Majesty has dispatched a Grand Marshal Hong, bearing an imperial vermilion edict and imperial incense, to come into the mountains and summon me to the Eastern Capital. There I am to conduct a Universal Offering of three thousand six hundred portions and pray for the removal of the pestilence throughout the realm. I shall now ride a crane and mount the clouds to go there.’ By this hour, I expect he has already gone and is no longer in the hermitage. You should not go up. The mountain is full of venomous creatures and savage beasts; I fear they may take your life.” The Grand Marshal asked again, “You had better not be lying.” The young attendant gave a laugh but made no reply; playing his iron flute once more, he passed around the mountain slope and disappeared. The Grand Marshal pondered, “How can that boy know everything about this affair? The Celestial Master must have told him. That must certainly be it.” He considered climbing farther, but the terror he had just endured had nearly cost him his life. Better to go back down the mountain, he decided.

p.src: The Grand Marshal took up the incense burner, found the old path again, and hurried down the mountain. The Taoists received him and invited him to sit in the abbot's quarters. The Perfected One asked the Grand Marshal, “Did you see the Celestial Master?” The Grand Marshal replied, “I am a high official of the imperial court. How could you make me walk these mountain paths and suffer such hardship? I very nearly lost my life. First, halfway up the mountain, a great white-browed tiger with glaring eyes leapt out and frightened the very soul from my body. Then, before I had passed the next spur, a huge snow-spotted serpent sprang from the bamboo and vines, coiled itself into a heap, and blocked my way. Had my good fortune not been so great, how could I ever have returned alive to the capital? It was all a trick played upon me by you Taoists.” The Perfected One answered, “How would humble Taoists such as ourselves dare slight a great minister? It was our Patriarch testing the Grand Marshal's heart. Though snakes and tigers live upon this mountain, they harm no one.” The Grand Marshal continued, “Just when I could walk no farther and was about to climb another slope, I saw a Taoist boy come around a pine tree, riding a yellow ox and playing an iron flute as he crossed the mountain. I asked him, ‘Where have you come from? Do you know who I am?’ He said, ‘I know all about it.’ He told me that, on the Celestial Master's instructions, the Master had ridden a crane through the clouds to the Eastern Capital that morning. That is why I returned.” The Perfected One said, “What a pity, Grand Marshal—you let him pass you by. That herdboy was the Celestial Master himself.” The Grand Marshal said, “If he was the Celestial Master, why did he look so wretched?” The Perfected One replied, “The Celestial Master of this generation is no ordinary person. Though young in years, his attainment in the Way is extraordinary. He stands beyond the common order of men, manifests his powers throughout the four quarters, and works wonders of the greatest efficacy. All the world calls him Patriarch Daotong.” Grand Marshal Hong said, “To think that I had eyes yet failed to recognize the true Master, and let him pass before my very face!” The Perfected One said, “Set your mind at ease, Grand Marshal. Since the Patriarch's sacred message says that he has gone, by the time you return to the capital he will already have completed the entire rite.” Only after hearing this did the Grand Marshal set his mind at ease. The Perfected One ordered a banquet prepared for the Grand Marshal, had the vermilion edict placed for safekeeping in an imperial document casket and left in the Palace of Supreme Purity, and had the imperial incense burned in the Hall of the Three Pure Ones. That day a great vegetarian feast was spread in the abbot's quarters, and they banqueted and drank until evening. When the feast ended, the Grand Marshal lodged there until dawn.

p.src: After the morning meal next day, the Perfected One, the Taoist community, the superintendent, and the temple attendants invited the Grand Marshal to tour the mountain. The Grand Marshal was delighted. A great company followed him as he walked out of the abbot's quarters, with two Taoist boys leading the way. They went before and behind the palace buildings, admiring the many sights. The splendor of the Hall of the Three Pure Ones was beyond all telling; beneath the left gallery stood the Hall of the Nine Heavens, the Hall of the Purple Tenuity, and the Hall of the North Pole; beneath the right gallery stood the Hall of Taiyi, the Hall of the Three Officials, and the Hall for the Expulsion of Evil. After viewing every hall, they came to a place behind the right gallery. When Grand Marshal Hong looked, he saw a separate hall surrounded on every side by walls of red clay mixed with pounded pepper; at the front were two vermilion lattice doors secured by a lock as thick as a man's arm, and more than ten sealing strips were pasted crosswise over them, each stamped over and over with vermilion seals; under the eaves hung a vermilion plaque inscribed in gold, with four golden characters written from the left: “Hall for the Subjugation of Demons.” Pointing at the doors, the Grand Marshal asked, “What place is this hall?” The Perfected One replied, “This is the hall in which the ancient ancestral Celestial Master imprisoned and subdued the Demon King.” The Grand Marshal asked again, “Why are so many seals pasted one upon another over it?” The Perfected One replied, “Our ancient patriarch, the Tang dynasty's State Preceptor Dongxuan, sealed the Demon King within this place. Whenever the office passed to a new Celestial Master, he personally added another seal, commanding that his descendants must never recklessly open it. Should the demon lord escape, the consequences would be dreadful. Eight or nine generations of patriarchs have now passed, and none has dared open it. The lock was cast by pouring molten bronze into it; who knows what lies within? This humble Taoist has presided over this palace for more than thirty years, yet I too have only heard tell of it.”

p.src: When Grand Marshal Hong heard this, he was filled with astonished curiosity and thought, “I shall have a look at this Demon King.” He said to the Perfected One, “Open the doors and let me see what the Demon King looks like.” The Perfected One pleaded, “Grand Marshal, we absolutely dare not open this hall! The ancestral Celestial Master left strict admonitions that no one in later generations was ever to open it without authority.” The Grand Marshal laughed. “Nonsense! You people wish to fabricate marvels and delude honest folk, so you deliberately arranged such a place and falsely claim that a Demon King is imprisoned here, all to parade your Taoist arts. I have read books that serve as a mirror to all things, yet never have I seen any method for imprisoning demons! Gods and ghosts belong to the hidden realm of darkness; I do not believe there is any Demon King inside. Open it for me at once, and let me see what this Demon King is like!” Again and again the Perfected One protested, “This hall must not be opened. We fear it will bring terrible consequences and harm people.” The Grand Marshal flew into a rage, pointed at the Taoists, and said, “If you do not open it for me to see, then when I return to court I shall first impeach all you Taoists for failing to obey the deadline of the imperial summons, defying the sacred decree, and preventing me from seeing the Celestial Master; then I shall report that you privately established this hall, falsely claiming to have imprisoned a Demon King in order to delude the soldiers and common people. I shall have every one of your ordination certificates revoked, tattoo you as criminals, and banish you to remote and pestilential military prefectures to suffer.”

p.src: Dim and silent, fathomless and dark; For hundreds of years no sunlight had entered, for countless ages no moonbeam had been seen. North could not be told from south—how could east be distinguished from west? Billowing black vapors struck men with cold; a shadowy chill pierced their bodies and made them tremble. A place no human footprint reached, a realm where demons and spirits roamed. Though one opened both eyes, one might as well be blind; though one stretched out both hands, one could not see one's palms. Always like the thirtieth night of the lunar month, forever like the hour before dawn.

p.src: They all entered the hall together, but in the darkness they could see nothing. The Grand Marshal ordered his attendants to light more than ten torches. When they brought them forward and shone them around, there was nothing on any side—only a stone stele in the center, some five or six feet high, seated upon a stone tortoise whose greater part was sunk in the mud. When they shone the light upon the face of the stele, it was covered with dragon-script and phoenix-seal characters, heavenly writing and talismanic signs, which no one could read; but when they illuminated the back, they found four great characters in standard script carved there: “To Be Opened When Hong Comes.” Was it not Heaven's decree that, first, the Stars of the Dipper were destined to enter the world; second, loyal and worthy men must arise in the Song dynasty; and third, by a wondrous coincidence Hong Xin should come upon this place? When Grand Marshal Hong saw the four characters, he was overjoyed and said to the Perfected One, “You tried to stop me, but how is it that my surname was already inscribed and ordained here hundreds of years ago? ‘To Be Opened When Hong Comes’ plainly commands me to open it and see. What harm can there be? I believe this Demon King can only be beneath the stone stele. You attendants, summon more of the Taoist laborers and bring hoes and iron spades to dig it open for me.”
